headline: Transit is Toronto's design language, and the best murals hide under expressways.
summary: Toronto's visual culture comes from infrastructure and diaspora: streetcar red, 1954 subway lettering, City Hall's 'eye' and Scarborough's board-formed concrete. More and more of the best makers work through Black-led and suburban hubs, after Artscape's collapse cut downtown studio space. Skip another CN Tower, maple leaf or OVO owl. Build a transit-and-concrete language with 416 and 905 artists instead.

insights.title: Toronto paints under its expressways
insights.detail: Many of the city's best-known walls are public infrastructure. StreetARToronto funds murals on underpasses and utility boxes. Painted pillars shade the Underpass Park basketball courts beneath the Eastern Ave and Adelaide/Richmond ramps. The Bentway runs art and a winter skate trail under the Gardiner's concrete bents. Graffiti Alley (Rush Lane, off Queen West) is still the showcase, where Elicser Elliott, Birdo and others have painted for years.
insights.implication: In Toronto the pier and the pillar are the native canvas. Design wraparound side-panel and shorts graphics as 'column murals' and commission them from StART-roster artists. Launch them on the Underpass Park courts, not at a downtown mall.

insights.title: The four bounces are back in play
insights.detail: Kawhi Leonard's Game 7 buzzer-beater over Philadelphia came on May 12, 2019. The crouch and the four rim bounces spread across GTA murals, tattoos and bootleg tees before the June 2019 title. His trade back from the Clippers this summer revives that imagery, now alongside 2026 All-Star Scottie Barnes.
insights.implication: Build the Kawhi-return drop around an abstract four-arc bounce graphic drawn by a Toronto artist, so there's no photograph to license. Pair it with product led by Barnes, so it reads as a new chapter and not a 2019 museum piece.

insights.title: The scene has left Queen West
insights.detail: Rising rents and Artscape Toronto's 2024 receivership squeezed downtown studio space. Black-led and suburban hubs gained ground: Nia Centre for the Arts on Oakwood Ave, BAND in Parkdale, Daniels Spectrum in Regent Park and Scarborough-rooted Mural Routes. So did MOCA, in the Junction Triangle's former Tower Automotive factory.
insights.implication: Find collaborators and run paid, credited co-design sessions through these hubs. Product should come from Oakwood, Regent Park and Scarborough, where much of the Raptors' fanbase lives, not from the downtown core.

insights.title: Transit is the GTA's shared typography
insights.detail: The 1954 Yonge line's custom geometric sans still names stations on tiled walls, and David Vereschagin digitized it as 'Toronto Subway'. The red-and-white streetcar is the 'Red Rocket'. Raptors 905 in Mississauga turned an area code into a team name. Fans place themselves by 416, 905 and their subway line.
insights.implication: A numbers-and-lettering system based on the subway face and the station tile bands would give Toronto a City Edition font no other market can copy. It needs a license from the TTC and from whoever holds the typeface rights.

insights.title: Diaspora craft is the city's textile tradition
insights.detail: Mas camps like Louis Saldenah's build feathered, beaded Carnival costumes all year for the August Grand Parade on Lake Shore Blvd. Brampton and Malton's Punjabi community wears phulkari embroidery at Vaisakhi. Little Ethiopia on the Danforth has tibeb woven borders and Ge'ez-script storefront signs.
insights.implication: Make each one a separate capsule, co-designed with named, paid community designers. Don't blend them into one 'multicultural' print. Time them to Black History Month in February, Vaisakhi in April and Carnival in August.

insights.title: The Raptors own red, black and purple
insights.detail: The Leafs, Blue Jays and Argonauts all dress the city in blue. The Raptors' visual history runs from the 1995 purple dinosaur of the Vince Carter era, through Sid Lee's black-and-white 2014 'We The North' campaign, to today's red, black and silver.
insights.implication: Use the contrast. Red and black for core product, Dino purple as the heritage lever for fans who grew up with Vince. Never default to a generic 'Toronto blue' that belongs to other franchises.

places.name: Graffiti Alley (Rush Lane)
places.why: This kilometre-long legal-wall laneway between Spadina and Portland is the city's densest record of its graffiti writers and muralists. Scout artists here first.

places.name: Underpass Park
places.kind: park with basketball courts and mural pillars
places.why: Its basketball half-courts sit under painted expressway pillars, the most direct meeting of Toronto hoops and Toronto murals.

places.name: The Bentway
places.kind: public art space under the Gardiner Expressway
places.why: It turns the Gardiner's concrete bents into a year-round venue for installations and a winter skate trail. It's a ready stage for column-graphic launches.

places.name: OCAD University (Sharp Centre for Design)
places.why: Canada's largest art and design university works from Will Alsop's checkerboard 'tabletop' on crayon-coloured stilts, beside Frank Gehry's AGO. Its students and alumni feed the city's illustration and design talent.

places.name: Museum of Contemporary Art Toronto (MOCA)
places.why: Housed in the former Tower Automotive factory, it anchors the west-end studio cluster that grew as galleries left Queen West.

places.name: Nia Centre for the Arts
places.neighborhood: Oakwood Village (Oakwood Ave, near Little Jamaica)
places.why: A centre for Black Canadian art and young creatives, and a natural co-design partner for Black History Month product.

places.name: Reggae Lane
places.why: Adrian Hayles's 2015 mural honours Toronto's reggae pioneers. It marks the heart of the Caribbean community, whose shops took years of damage from Crosstown construction.

places.name: Daniels Spectrum
places.why: The arts centre of the rebuilt Regent Park, home to community arts organizations. It's the place to co-create with east-downtown youth.

places.name: Scarborough Civic Centre
places.why: Raymond Moriyama's 1973 white concrete civic building is Scarborough's architectural signature. It has hosted Nuit Blanche exhibitions.

places.name: Sankofa Square (formerly Yonge-Dundas Square)
places.why: The city's billboard-lit crossroads, renamed for the Akan concept of sankofa, sits under the restored spinning-record neon of Sam the Record Man.

people.name: Elicser Elliott
people.why: His expressive figures of everyday, often Black and brown, Torontonians cover Graffiti Alley and Kensington. He's a credible voice for player and fan portraiture.

people.name: Adrian Hayles
people.why: He painted Reggae Lane in Little Jamaica. His community-centred, figurative murals suit Caribbean-diaspora Raptors stories.

people.name: Clandestinos (Shalak Attack and Bruno Smoky)
people.why: This Toronto-based, Latin American-rooted duo paints vivid large-scale murals across the city, with the scale and colour to work as wraparound uniform graphics.

people.name: Esmaa Mohamoud
people.why: Her concrete basketballs and reworked jerseys question how Black athletes are seen and sold, which makes her the most serious basketball artist in the market. Give her editorial control of any collaboration.

people.name: Louis Saldenah
people.role: Mas band leader and costume designer (Saldenah Carnival)
people.why: His band has won Toronto Carnival's Band of the Year many times. He's the leading name in the city's feather, bead and sequin craft.

people.name: Peace Collective
people.why: Its 'Toronto vs Everybody' tees became the city's unofficial fan uniform, and showed how badly people here want local-pride graphics.

people.name: StreetARToronto (StART)
people.role: City of Toronto street art program
people.why: It funds and manages murals on underpasses, laneways and utility boxes, and is the gateway to the city's muralist roster and its walls.

people.name: Mural Routes
people.why: This Scarborough-rooted group trains muralists and produces community murals across the inner suburbs. It's a partner for 416-and-905 product.

moments.name: DesignTO Festival
moments.why: A citywide design festival of window installations and exhibitions, and a mid-season platform to show a Raptors design process.

moments.name: Winter Stations
moments.why: A design competition that turns lifeguard stands on the east-end beaches into winter art installations. It's a Toronto-only cold-weather design story.

moments.name: Four-bounce anniversary (Kawhi's 2019 Game 7 winner)
moments.why: With Kawhi back, the anniversary of Toronto's most-reproduced sports image could fall in a playoff run.

moments.name: CONTACT Photography Festival
moments.why: A month-long citywide photography festival with large outdoor public installations. Scout photographers here and stage player-portrait works.

moments.name: Toronto Outdoor Art Fair
moments.why: This long-running juried outdoor fair at Nathan Phillips Square is the best single scouting ground for local illustrators and printmakers.

moments.name: Toronto Caribbean Carnival Grand Parade
moments.timing: Early August, Simcoe Day long weekend
moments.why: The mas camps' year of costume-building peaks on Lake Shore Blvd, in the city's biggest design spectacle.

moments.name: Nuit Blanche Toronto
moments.why: An all-night contemporary art event downtown and, in recent editions, the inner suburbs. It falls weeks before tip-off.

moments.name: Art Toronto
moments.why: Canada's main international art fair, at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, lands in tip-off week. That makes it an art-world stage for a season-opening drop.

vocabulary.meaning: Toronto, popularized by Drake around 2015. It's all over souvenir merch, so it fails the swap test for premium product.
Area codes used as identity: 416 is the city and 905 the suburbs (Mississauga, Brampton, Markham, Vaughan). The G League affiliate is literally named Raptors 905.
Nickname for TTC vehicles, especially the red-and-white streetcars.
The Raptors' rallying cry and brand platform since 2014, created with agency Sid Lee. It claims all of Canada as the team's turf.
The outdoor watch party in Maple Leaf Square outside Scotiabank Arena. During the 2019 run, squares across Canada copied it, from Mississauga to Halifax.
A Mohawk-derived name for the area, usually translated as 'where there are trees standing in the water'. It appears in land acknowledgements and Indigenous art, and it's not a free-to-use slogan.
A Carnival band's workshop, where costumes are designed and built for months before the Grand Parade.
Peace Collective's underdog-pride slogan, now shorthand for the city's chip on its shoulder. It's their IP, not a public phrase.

designCues.cue: Red Rocket red: the flat TTC streetcar red set against white and black, as on the Flexity and retired CLRV liveries.
designCues.source: TTC streetcars and corporate red (approximate; match to TTC brand standards)
designCues.use: Trim, piping and taping on warm-ups and shooting shirts, set against Raptors red #CE1141 as a deliberate tonal clash. Using the streetcar silhouette or TTC marks requires a license.

designCues.cue: Toronto Subway lettering: the squared, wide-countered geometric sans in all caps on the walls of the original Yonge and Bloor-Danforth stations.
designCues.source: TTC Line 1 and Line 2 station walls, digitized as the 'Toronto Subway' typeface by David Vereschagin
designCues.use: Jersey numbers, name bars and wordmarks. Either license the revival or have a Toronto type designer draw an original face in its spirit.

designCues.cue: Glossy two-tone station tile walls, where each original subway station has its own colour pairing and the station name runs in a contrasting band.
designCues.source: Original Yonge (1954) and Bloor-Danforth (1966) subway stations
designCues.use: Gridded tile texture on side panels, plus a 'home stop' capsule where each colourway is a station a fan grew up on.

designCues.cue: City Hall's 'eye': two curved towers cupping a round council chamber.
designCues.source: Viljo Revell's 1965 Toronto City Hall, abstracted in the Toronto flag and city logo
designCues.use: Abstract the curve-pair-plus-disc into a neck tape, waistband or hangtag motif. Don't reproduce the official logo or flag without City of Toronto permission.

designCues.cue: Board-formed concrete and the balcony grid of postwar slab towers, in heathered concrete grey (about #8C8C88).
designCues.source: Moriyama's Scarborough Civic Centre, Robarts Library and the slab towers of St. James Town, Thorncliffe Park and Jane & Finch
designCues.use: Concrete-heather knits and a balcony-grid all-over print. Co-design them with artists from those neighbourhoods so they read as pride, not 'urban decay'.

designCues.cue: Dino purple: the original Raptors purple of the jagged-pinstripe, dinosaur-dribbling 1995 uniforms.
designCues.source: Raptors' 1995-era identity and the Vince Carter years
designCues.use: Heritage colourway lever for millennial fans. Pair it sparingly with black and Raptors red #CE1141, and don't add the full throwback dinosaur to everything.

designCues.cue: Yonge Street marquee neon: Sam the Record Man's twin spinning red-neon records and the bulb-lit, hand-lettered pun signs of the vanished Honest Ed's.
designCues.source: Yonge Street and Bloor-Bathurst retail signage, now civic nostalgia
designCues.use: Neon-tube outline lettering and bulb-dot typography for holiday and playoff tees. The signs themselves are third-party property, so borrow the technique, not the marks.

designCues.cue: Phulkari: dense geometric darning-stitch 'flower work' in golden silk floss (about #E1A730) on red or rust cotton (about #9E1B32).
designCues.source: Punjabi community of Brampton and Malton, worn at Vaisakhi and weddings
designCues.use: Embroidered trim or a chest patch for a Brampton capsule, co-designed with Punjabi-Canadian designers and stitched by South Asian makers. Keep religious symbols such as the Khanda off product.

productHooks: 'Four Bounces' Kawhi-return capsule: an abstract four-arc bounce graphic drawn by a Toronto muralist such as Elicser Elliott. Release it for Kawhi's 2026-27 home debut, with a matching mural on the Underpass Park courts. No licensed photograph needed.

'Line 1 / Line 2' lettering kit: Raptors names and numbers in a subway-inspired face, with station-tile side panels. License it through the TTC and sell it in station-specific colourways at a Union Station pop-up.

'416 / 905' capsule: paired city and suburb tees and shooting shirts with a balcony-grid all-over print. Co-design it through Mural Routes in Scarborough and launch it with Raptors 905 in Mississauga.

Black History Month collection with Nia Centre artists, or with Esmaa Mohamoud on her terms: concrete-textured ball and jersey graphics. Credit and pay the artists, and share proceeds with the partner hub.
Brampton Vaisakhi capsule, timed to mid-April during the playoff push: phulkari-embroidered trim on Raptors red and black, made with Punjabi-Canadian designers and makers.
Tip-off art series for late October around Art Toronto: limited artist tees from Clandestinos, Adrian Hayles and other StART muralists, launched under the Gardiner at The Bentway or at MOCA.
watchouts: Swap-test traps: the CN Tower skyline, a generic red maple leaf and 'The 6ix' are on every souvenir rack. Leaning on Drake and OVO as Toronto's only visual voice is also risky while his public feuds and lawsuit play out.

Third-party IP needs licensing. That covers TTC logos, streetcar livery and the 'Toronto Subway' revival font, plus the City of Toronto logo and flag. It covers the Sam the Record Man and Honest Ed's signs and Hudson's Bay's multistripe, now owned by Canadian Tire. Getty/NBAE photos of the 2019 Game 7 shot, Universal's 'Jurassic Park' film marks and Peace Collective's slogans need clearing too.

Toronto sits on Treaty 13 and Dish With One Spoon territory. Wampum belts, medicine wheels and eagle feathers are sacred or treaty objects. Any 'Tkaronto' product needs engagement with the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation and named, paid Indigenous artists.
Diaspora textiles (mas, phulkari, tibeb, kente) belong to specific communities. Co-design, credit and pay. Avoid patois punchlines, flag-and-dreadlocks Jamaican clichés and religious symbols.

Artists here are under pressure: Artscape's collapse and Little Jamaica's losses from Crosstown construction are recent wounds. Pay real fees, never ask for 'exposure' murals, and don't sell Little Jamaica's look while its businesses are still recovering.
